Hi again Mark,

> 1. I think you have to specify the yearlySiteCovs:
>
> ammaMF <- formatLong(amma, type = "unmarkedMultFrame", numPrimary = 5, yearlySiteCovs = visit)

Please see Dan Linden's nice description of these types of covariates <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/unmarked/TrZD8Oxj-OM/AkZQSeZZwZMJ>. A yearlySiteCov is a variable the varies among sites in a given year, and within a site(s) over multiple years.

None of your covariates fits this description and, as such, you do not have any yearlySiteCovs.

FWCPdata <- read.csv("~/FWS_Projects/sandbox/Data/FWCPDataLongTsp.csv", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  # Drop records with no response; we'll complete data set below
  filter(!is.na <http://is.na>(y))

# Explore covariate temporal variation within sites
cov_temp <- group_by(FWCPdata, site) %>%
  summarise_at(vars(place.1, vri.2, wetdist.3, cutdist.4, rddist.5), n_distinct)
summary(cov_temp)
#>      site              place.1      vri.2     wetdist.3   cutdist.4

> 2. The covariates need to be transformed. I note in your teaching post that you had done the following:

The covariates don't necessarily need to be transformed, but it can improve computation efficiency/speed in some case. I applied an slightly unusual transformation in that example for various reasons. You can use whatever approach makes most sense---no transformation, more typical approaches (see `?scale`), etc...

> Why is cutdist.4 in my obsCov and not in siteCovs? JulianDate is still being introduced.

`JulianDate` is simply what `formatLong` calls the variable you denoted as the "observation number" variable. In your case, this was `visit`. Thus, `JulianDate` is simply the same thing as what was originally called `visit`.

Best,
Adam

I'm hoping someone can provide some insight into my goodness of fit results.
I'm using Occu() function and I'm interested in detection probabilities of 11 species from my very large camera trap survey. I have ~40 sampling occasions (7 days per occasion) and ~1000 sites.

When testing goodness of fit with mb.gof.test with nsim=1000, some species have chat values that look okay, but other species have chat values in the thousands, and two species that output chat=Inf.....maybe that just means my models dont adequately fit the data, but it seems rather outrageous to get chat values in the thousands or infinite chat, which leads me to believe I'm making some sort of error somewhere?

The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...
If anyone can provide some insight, I would be extremely appreciative!

Best regards,
Carly

Dear Carly,

to this, "The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...", a cynic might simply comment that GoF tests are often merely a test of whether your sample size is big enough to detect the violation of your model's assumptions.

But more seriously, yes, basically, a high value of the test statistic says that your data are extraordinary under the parametric assumptions of your model. And I would think that a result of infinity means that somewhere along the calculations to arrive at that test statistic there was a division by zero. Or perhaps some value that became too small or too large for R.

One thing that came to my mind is that 40 occasions is huge. I would never fit an occupancy model to such data, although this is of course not wrong. But I think that you can gain a lot by lumping your data, say, into 4 occasions of 10 days each. This will make detection probability higher (which is always a good thing with capture-recapture methods) and moreover, it will tend to reduce temporal autocorrelation in your response. This latter may be one of the mechanisms that contribute to the lack of fit of your data: when animals move around in some area, perhaps they hang our in the area of one trap for a couple days and then move on. This will result in a tendency of 1's to be followed by 1's at a given trap (and 0's by 0's), which is a violation of the usual assumption of independence. It could be addressed by modeling trap-dependence, but if you can make it go away, then that would be even better.

I am sure that this is at best a partial remedy to your problems, but I would explore this avenue a little.

Best regards --  Marc

to this, "The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...", a cynic might simply comment that GoF tests are often merely a test of whether your sample size is big enough to detect the violation of your model's assumptions.

But more seriously, yes, basically, a high value of the test statistic says that your data are extraordinary under the parametric assumptions of your model. And I would think that a result of infinity means that somewhere along the calculations to arrive at that test statistic there was a division by zero. Or perhaps some value that became too small or too large for R.

One thing that came to my mind is that 40 occasions is huge. I would never fit an occupancy model to such data, although this is of course not wrong. But I think that you can gain a lot by lumping your data, say, into 4 occasions of 10 days each. This will make detection probability higher (which is always a good thing with capture-recapture methods) and moreover, it will tend to reduce temporal autocorrelation in your response. This latter may be one of the mechanisms that contribute to the lack of fit of your data: when animals move around in some area, perhaps they hang our in the area of one trap for a couple days and then move on. This will result in a tendency of 1's to be followed by 1's at a given trap (and 0's by 0's), which is a violation of the usual assumption of independence. It could be addressed by modeling trap-dependence, but if you can make it go away, then that would be even better.

I am sure that this is at best a partial remedy to your problems, but I would explore this avenue a little.

Best regards --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to generate results from a Generalized Multinomial N-mixture Model (GMM) and following a mixture of scripts from the {unmarked} package's help files as well as this thread on the Google Group: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c.

I'm interested in fitting the GMM to imaginary data, assuming a dependent double-observer approach with 2 (or more) observers (e.g., representing interannual technician turnover) in a hypothetical survey that would have 10 primary (e.g., years) and 5 secondary (e.g., replicate surveys per year, across a breeding season) periods.

I'm also interested in adding both observer ID and Julian date as observation-level covariates in the model, but I just can't seem to get the dimensions right for occasions or observer IDs in my current tests.

Here's a snippet of my code:

########################################################################

# Example for setting up data with covariates and without fitting a model
library(unmarked)
n <- 100 #Number of sites
T <- 10 #Number of primary periods
J <- 5 #Number of secondary periods
site <- 1:100 #Site IDs
years <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2010:2019, each=n), n, T)) #Matrix of years surveyed
years <- data.frame(lapply(years, as.factor)) #Factorize the years
y <- array(rpois(n*J*T,3), c(n, 2, T)) #Matrix of counts with approximate lambda of 3 (i.e. expected local abundance per location)
occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:(J*T), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of sampling occasions (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)
observers <- data.frame(matrix(rep(c("A","B"), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of observer IDs (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)

#doublepiFun; see: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c
depDoubleObs <- function(p) {
  M <- nrow(p)
  pi <- matrix(NA, M, 2)
  pi[,1] <- p[,1]
  pi[,2] <- p[,2]*(1-p[,1])
  return(pi)
}
obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)
numPrimary <- T
obsToY <- kronecker(diag(numPrimary), obsToY)

#Setting up the object frame
umfGMM <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y,
                            siteCovs = data.frame(site=site),
                            obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions, observer=observers),
                            yearlySiteCovs=data.frame(year=c(t(years))),
                            numPrimary=T, type="double", obsToY=obsToY,
                            piFun="depDoubleObs")
##Error thrown: Error in unmarkedFrame(y, siteCovs, obsCovs, obsToY = obsToY) :
##At least one matrix in obsCovs has incorrect number of dimensions.

########################################################################

Would anyone be willing and able to help me resolve this error? Also, would the final umfGMM be readily amenable to the Dail-Madsen frame and model (i.e. unmarkedFramePCO and pcountOpen)?

I suspect that if the dimensions of both occasions and observer IDs are corrected, then adding a new covariate like Julian date to the GMM would be relatively straightforward. I must admit that I regularly struggle with justifying object dimensionality for these kinds of tools, unfortunately.

Thanks for any help, in advance!

Yes, I misunderstood the original framework (you do not need to run dynamic models if sites were not run in a repeated framework), but I would still recommend trying a dynamic model for the 6 months that the cameras were out, especially since I think you are capturing end of spring, summer, beginning of fall, which might exhibit differences in behavior, resources use, and movement of the species of interest. I think it's important to remember the assumptions of a single-season occupancy model (closure), especially in the context of a camera trap and the defined "site". I doubt that these sites are closed during the 6-month period, and much of the issues with detectability in camera trap surveys are confounded by that availability (e.g., temporary emigration), so I think you would have much more luck fitting models by accounting for those dynamics. Hope that helps!

Cheers,

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

The dependent double observer approach with gmultmix() expects exactly two "secondary periods" within each primary period; that is, the counts from the two observers. You have to restructure a few things in the code to make that work, starting with changing J = 2:

n <- 100 #Number of sites
T <- 10 #Number of primary periods

J <- 2 #Number of secondary periods

site <- 1:100 #Site IDs
years <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2010:2019, each=n), n, T)) #Matrix of years surveyed
years <- data.frame(lapply(years, as.factor)) #Factorize the years

y <- array(rpois(n*J*T,3), c(n, J * T)) #Matrix of counts with approximate lambda of 3 (i.e. expected local abundance per location)
occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:T, each=n*J), n, J*T)) #Matrix of sampling occasions (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)

observers <- data.frame(matrix(rep(c("A","B"), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of observer IDs (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)

In this new setup the y matrix is dimensions (100, 2*T) and the column order is occasion1observer1, occasion1observer2, occasion2observer1 ....
Also you want to provide either the type argument or obsToY/piFun arguments to unmarkedFrameGMM, but not both (in your case, the latter:

#Setting up the object frame
umfGMM <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y,
                            siteCovs = data.frame(site=site),
                            obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions, observer=observers),
                            yearlySiteCovs=data.frame(year=c(t(years))),

                            numPrimary=T, obsToY=obsToY,
                            piFun="depDoubleObs")

With these changes I was able to construct the unmarkedFrame.

Based on your description of the hypothetical survey it also sounds like maybe what you actually want is 10 primary periods (years) each with 5 secondary periods (within years) and then within *each of those* 5 secondary periods you actually conduct the dependent double observer sampling. I don't think it is possible to fit such a model in unmarked. You can either estimate temporary emigration/availability with gmultmix() or between-year population dynamics with pcountOpen(), but not both at the same time. I could be wrong about this! One thing that probably adds to the confusion is that unmarkedFrameGMM has the "yearlySiteCovs" argument which as Richard noted should probably actually be called "primarySiteCovs" (https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/issues/38).

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marconi,

I think you are seeing that error because you are trying to generated a model-averaged prediction using a raster as the newdata. This is still currently not supported in unmarked. If this is the case you can try converting your raster to a data frame as Richard suggests.

Alternatively I wrote up a quick function that should allow for predicting from fitlists with a raster, while still getting a raster output. See example below based on Richard's spatial vignette. It seems to work for me - I'll write a patch to get it into the next version of unmarked so this is handled automatically.

Ken

Example:

library(unmarked)
library(raster)
data(crossbill)
data(Switzerland)

#Fit two models
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(
y=as.matrix(crossbill[,c("det991", "det992", "det993")]),
siteCovs=crossbill[,c("ele", "forest")],
obsCovs=list(date=crossbill[,c("date991", "date992", "date993")]))

sc <- scale(siteCovs(umf))
siteCovs(umf) <- sc

fm.occu <- occu(~date ~ele + I(ele^2) + forest, umf)

fm.occu2 <- occu(~1~1, umf)

#Build newdata raster stack
elevation <- rasterFromXYZ(Switzerland[,c("x","y","elevation")],
    crs="+proj=somerc +lat_0=46.95240555555556 +lon_0=7.439583333333333 +k_0=1 +x_0=600000 +y_0=200000 +ellps=bessel +towgs84=674.374,15.056,405.346,0,0,0,0 +units=m +no_defs")

forest <- rasterFromXYZ(Switzerland[,c("x","y","forest")],
    crs="+proj=somerc +lat_0=46.95240555555556 +lon_0=7.439583333333333 +k_0=1 +x_0=600000 +y_0=200000 +ellps=bessel +towgs84=674.374,15.056,405.346,0,0,0,0 +units=m +no_defs")

ele.s <- (elevation-1189)/640
forest.s <- (forest-34.7)/27.7
ef <- stack(ele.s, forest.s)
names(ef) <- c("ele", "forest")

#Make fitlist
fl = fitList(fm.occu,fm.occu2)

#New function for model-averaged prediction from a fitList using a raster input
pred_raster_fitlist <- function(object, type, newdata=NULL,
    backTransform = TRUE, appendData = FALSE, level=0.95){

  #----Same as existing function
  fl <- object@fits
  ese <- lapply(fl, predict, type = type, newdata = newdata,
                backTransform = backTransform, level=level)
  #---------------------------------

  if(class(newdata) == "RasterStack"){
    if(!require(raster)) stop("raster package is required")
    ese <- lapply(ese, as.matrix)
  }

  #----Same as existing function
  E <- sapply(ese, function(x) x[,"Predicted"])
  SE <- sapply(ese, function(x) x[,"SE"])
  lower <- sapply(ese, function(x) x[,"lower"])
  upper <- sapply(ese, function(x) x[,"upper"])
  ic <- sapply(fl, slot, "AIC")
  deltaic <- ic - min(ic)
  wts <- exp(-deltaic / 2)
  wts <- wts / sum(wts)
  parav <- as.numeric(E %*% wts)
  seav <- as.numeric(sqrt(SE^2 + (E - parav)^2) %*% wts)
  out <- data.frame(Predicted = parav, SE = seav)
  out$lower <- as.numeric(lower %*% wts)
  out$upper <- as.numeric(upper %*% wts)
  #------------------------------

  if(class(newdata) == "RasterStack"){
    E.mat <- matrix(out[,1], dim(newdata)[1], dim(newdata)[2], byrow=TRUE)
    E.raster <- raster::raster(E.mat)
    raster::extent(E.raster) <- raster::extent(newdata)
    out.rasters <- list(E.raster)
    for(i in 2:ncol(out)) {
      i.mat <- matrix(out[,i], dim(newdata)[1], dim(newdata)[2], byrow=TRUE)
      i.raster <- raster::raster(i.mat)
      raster::extent(i.raster) <- raster::extent(newdata)
      out.rasters[[i]] <- i.raster
    }
    out.stack <- stack(out.rasters)
    names(out.stack) <- colnames(out)
    raster::crs(out.stack) <- raster::crs(newdata)
    return(out.stack)
  }
}

#Generate model-averaged prediction
raster_test <- pred_raster_fitlist(fl, type='state', newdata=ef)
plot(raster_test)

> I am attempting to generate results from a Generalized Multinomial N-mixture Model (GMM) and following a mixture of scripts from the {unmarked} package's help files as well as this thread on the Google Group: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c.
>
> I'm interested in fitting the GMM to imaginary data, assuming a dependent double-observer approach with 2 (or more) observers (e.g., representing interannual technician turnover) in a hypothetical survey that would have 10 primary (e.g., years) and 5 secondary (e.g., replicate surveys per year, across a breeding season) periods.
>
> I'm also interested in adding both observer ID and Julian date as observation-level covariates in the model, but I just can't seem to get the dimensions right for occasions or observer IDs in my current tests.
>
> Here's a snippet of my code:
>
> ########################################################################
>
> # Example for setting up data with covariates and without fitting a model
> library(unmarked)
> n <- 100 #Number of sites
> T <- 10 #Number of primary periods
> J <- 5 #Number of secondary periods
> site <- 1:100 #Site IDs
> years <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2010:2019, each=n), n, T)) #Matrix of years surveyed
> years <- data.frame(lapply(years, as.factor)) #Factorize the years
> y <- array(rpois(n*J*T,3), c(n, 2, T)) #Matrix of counts with approximate lambda of 3 (i.e. expected local abundance per location)
> occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:(J*T), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of sampling occasions (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)
> observers <- data.frame(matrix(rep(c("A","B"), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of observer IDs (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)
>
> #doublepiFun; see: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c
> depDoubleObs <- function(p) {
>   M <- nrow(p)
>   pi <- matrix(NA, M, 2)
>   pi[,1] <- p[,1]
>   pi[,2] <- p[,2]*(1-p[,1])
>   return(pi)
> }
> obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)
> numPrimary <- T
> obsToY <- kronecker(diag(numPrimary), obsToY)
>
> #Setting up the object frame
> umfGMM <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y,
>                             siteCovs = data.frame(site=site),
>                             obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions, observer=observers),
>                             yearlySiteCovs=data.frame(year=c(t(years))),
>                             numPrimary=T, type="double", obsToY=obsToY,
>                             piFun="depDoubleObs")
> ##Error thrown: Error in unmarkedFrame(y, siteCovs, obsCovs, obsToY = obsToY) :
> ##At least one matrix in obsCovs has incorrect number of dimensions.
>
> ########################################################################
>
> Would anyone be willing and able to help me resolve this error? Also, would the final umfGMM be readily amenable to the Dail-Madsen frame and model (i.e. unmarkedFramePCO and pcountOpen)?
>
> I suspect that if the dimensions of both occasions and observer IDs are corrected, then adding a new covariate like Julian date to the GMM would be relatively straightforward. I must admit that I regularly struggle with justifying object dimensionality for these kinds of tools, unfortunately.
>
> Thanks for any help, in advance!

The link that Ken gives is definitely useful for get measures of multicollinearity.  But to state what maybe isn't always obvious:  there is really no such thing as "accounting for" or "controlling for" multicollinearity with the same data set.  For example is distance to water is highly correlated with elevation, then one can't drop one of those variables and then claim causal inferences about the variable that remains in the model.  Removing variables that are correlated can certainly result in fewer models being examined without much loss of predictive ability and produce more numerically stable models.

So knowing the level and where multicollinearity exists in the data is a good thing to know.  It's just that with the same data set unambiguous inferences about certain coefficients aren't possible if variables are tossed out based on tests of multicollinearity.

My apologies if I've just stated the obvious.

Jim

Attached is R Code for another demonstration of a customized unmarked function (i.e., hack).   In this case, I have altered the "occu" function two do two things:

1) accept single visit, continuous time to detection data
2) use a complementary log-log link for occupancy, so that abundance can be derived.

This model is useful if, instead of repeat visits, you visit each plot once for a longer period of time and record the time when you first detected the species.  It could also be useful for camera trap data, which are really from continuous sensors.  But maybe that bears further discussion.  I tested this model against a Bayesian version from the AHM book (p. 615-617) and got the same results with both methods.  But if you can find bugs or errors let me know.

I have attached an R Script containing a bunch of unmarked functions that you have to run locally, first, to make the occu.cttd function work.  The R code includes the data simulator, and a comparison of the analytical results to the simulation values.

• Closed-population models for population size
• Cormack-Jolly-Seber models for survival probabilities
• Multistate capture-recapture models for survival and transition rates
• Site-occupancy models (MacKenzie et al. 2002, 2003) for the analysis of species distributions
• Binomial mixture models (Royle 2004) for the analysis of distribution and abundance with full accounting for observation error

Abundance might well induce more heterogeneity in detection across spatial replicates than temporal replicates in certain situations. If there's some reason to suspect serial correlation in observations or other dependence, the Hines 2010 model might be appropriate, or if you can figure out how to fit it, you could consider the approach from this paper which is kind of the RN analogue (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00159.x).

W/r/t counts, not quite sure what you mean--or maybe not sure what the reviewer means. Presumably you've reduced the counts to 0/1 when fitting the occupancy model. Maybe a majority of studies that estimate occupancy collapse some sort of count of observations within a temporal interval (e.g., trail cameras, bird point counts, etc.)?

Cheers,

John

Dear Eric,

I would do this:
- from n sites surveyed over multiple years, sample with replacement n sites. Hence, some sites will appear in the bootstrap data multiple times and some sites not at all.
- then do the stacking and fit the model, save the MLEs (no need for SEs --- speeds things up)
- repeat this 1000 or so times and take the SD as the bootstrap SE and a 95% percentile as a bootstrapped 95% CI

That's what we do in the upcoming AHM2 book too.

Best regards  --- Marc
